summary:
Belize decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2016, and the ruling governs the legal position a visitor faces. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, in a judgment delivered by Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, struck down Section 53 of the Criminal Code, a colonial-era sodomy provision, as unconstitutional. The challenge was filed in 2010 by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco through the advocacy organisation UNIBAM and heard in Belize City in 2013. Human Dignity Trust records the case among the constitutional challenges to laws criminalising same-sex activity that it documents across the region.

Belize was the first former British Caribbean colony to overturn its anti-sodomy law, a standing that has shaped how the country is described to travellers. The same body of commentary stresses that the statute had been rarely enforced before 2016 yet still fostered intolerance, and it points to a 1998 protest against a gay cruise docking as evidence of hostility that outlasts the statute itself.

Under the Universal Periodic Review in 2018 Belize accepted 15 of 17 recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity, the largest acceptance by any CARICOM state at that point. The accepted recommendations carry pledges of legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, training for the police, and collection of SOGI data. Two recommendations concerned with equality of rights and were merely 'noted' rather than accepted, leaving that part of the reform package without a government commitment.

The consequence axis of an arrest remains undocumented. The one prison-oriented source in this record, the survey of LGBTQ people in prison, returns no usable finding for Belize: no birth-sex versus identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no recorded solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. Where a detained trans visitor would therefore be housed is unknown, and with no legal gender recognition available the silence cannot be read as a protective standard.
tangentialFactors:
Belize's decriminalisation came through the courts rather than the legislature, which means the surrounding framework, including any hate-crime provision or gender-recognition procedure, has not been rebuilt alongside it. The country was a regional outlier in both directions: first in the former British Caribbean to strike down a sodomy law, and among the more accommodating CARICOM states in accepting SOGI recommendations at the 2018 Universal Periodic Review.

The organised presence of UNIBAM, the organisation behind the Orozco litigation, gives a trans visitor an identifiable local point of contact, which is not typical across the small states of the region. Social acceptance does not track the legal change evenly; the commentary covering expatriate life reports that gay travellers have long found Belize friendly while recording residual public hostility of the kind seen in the 1998 docking protest.

Gun and gang violence in Belize City is a general public-safety condition rather than a trans-specific risk, but it shapes where a visitor spends time and how quickly police respond. Ordinary crime reporting in the city does not distinguish victims by gender identity, so no separate figure for trans-specific violence exists in this record.
localsOnly:
Residents live under a constitutional right that struck down Section 53, but the practical protections around it are still being built. The 2018 Universal Periodic Review commitments include explicit anti-discrimination legislation and police training on sexual orientation and gender identity, and the record also carries employment protection against discrimination on those grounds, which governs how a resident can raise a complaint at work.

Legal gender recognition is not available, so residents cannot change the sex marker on birth certificates, passports or national identity documents. The resulting mismatch between documents and presentation is a daily administrative burden that falls on residents more than on short-term visitors, and it is the condition most likely to surface at a bank, a clinic or a government counter.

UNIBAM functions as the standing advocacy body, having carried the Orozco case from filing in 2010 to judgment in 2016, and it is the principal route for a resident seeking to escalate a discrimination or policing complaint. The pledge to collect SOGI data accepted in 2018 would, if implemented, give residents the first official statistics on violence and service access; no such dataset appears in this record.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the anti-discrimination legislation pledged at the 2018 Universal Periodic Review has since been enacted is unresolved in this record. The inventory carries the pledge and separately reflects employment protection, but it does not contain the statute text or a commencement date, so the two are not reconciled here.

No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, hate-crime enhancement, or the treatment of gender identity in asylum and refugee screening. Those gaps are stated as unsourced rather than as confirmed absences, except for gender recognition, which the record carries as unavailable.

Enforcement of the 2016 ruling below the Supreme Court is not evidenced: there is no material here on arrests brought under Section 53 after August 2016, on appellate review, or on how police apply the judgment in practice. Likewise, no data exists in this record on violence against trans people specifically, whether reported to police or to community organisations.

The prison question is unresolved on its own terms. The single source consulted is a general survey whose only Belize reference is a navigation link, so it cannot confirm or exclude any particular housing or segregation practice for a detained trans person.
